title: A Bombay lawyer never performed music in public. He's the reason Indian classical music has a written notation at all.

sources.text: Ramesh Gangolli - Chatura Pandit: V.N. Bhatkhande

caption:
A Bombay lawyer never performed music in public. He's the reason Indian classical music has a written notation at all.

Bhatkhande, born in Bombay in 1860, trained as a lawyer - Elphinstone College, a law degree and practice at the Bombay and Karachi High Courts - before abandoning law to spend decades documenting Hindustani classical music.

His six-volume Kramik Pustak Malika recorded over 1,850 compositions using a notation system he invented himself, after travelling India to persuade hereditary musicians to share compositions their families had guarded orally for generations.

He edited his final volumes from his sickbed after a stroke in 1933, working until his death. A student in any Indian music school today who names a raga's thaat is using a system built by a man who kept a promise to stay off the stage.
